title: Persistent post-pandemic labor-force exit is concentrated among low-income and low-skill US workers
source_unit: US tax-panel workers, occupation, income, labor-force exit, self-employment income, wages, benefits, stimulus, and post-pandemic work preferences

observations.period: Working paper issued October 2026; post-COVID recession labor-market panel

denominator.unit: US tax-data panel of workers with occupation information; exact sample count not disclosed in the NBER abstract

labor_force_exit.unit: persistent labor-force exit is especially concentrated among low-income and low-skill workers

highest_exit_group.unit: low-skilled unmarried men are the group most likely to exit

missing_income_replacement.unit: people leaving the labor force do not on average replace the missing income

self_employment_replacement.unit: approximate percent of lost W-2 income replaced by self-employment income

proposed_explanations.unit: little evidence that school closures, virus exposure, stimulus payments, unemployment benefits, occupation upgrading, or firm quality explain the exits

work_preferences.unit: facts are consistent with lower willingness to work for low pay and greater preferences for leisure and job flexibility

observations.method: A tax-data panel with newly assembled occupation information tracks workers across the post-pandemic labor market and compares exit, income replacement, occupation, firm quality, and candidate explanations.
observations.uncertainty: The NBER abstract does not disclose panel size, effect sizes, exact exit definition, observation window, or all identification assumptions. Reported preference interpretations are not direct randomized measures; tax data may miss informal work, household transfers, care work, health, and subjective wellbeing.
observations.subgroup: Low-income and low-skill workers, especially low-skilled unmarried men, compared with other workers and income groups.
observations.counterinterpretation: Exit can reflect disability, caregiving, housing, local labor demand, informal work, partner income, wealth, immigration, or reporting changes; self-employment income is not equivalent to stable earnings, benefits, worker voice, or job quality.

related_sources.claim: Minimum-wage hours effects differ for recently arrived immigrant workers while employment does not show a reported decline.
Minimum wages have adverse reported employment, hours, and earnings effects for initially-employed low-wage workers in poor and low-income families.
AI-skilled employment and organization capital are associated with recent firm productivity growth, leaving worker conversion open.

boundary: This record adds a post-pandemic labor-force exit and income-replacement layer to the US work/consumer program. It does not establish why workers exit, whether exit is harmful or voluntary, or how informal work, care, health, benefits, household resources, and later re-entry evolve.
